problem.summary: 标准深度学习方法在需要多步、高层推理的视觉推理任务（如CLEVR基准）上表现不佳，往往利用数据偏差而非捕获复杂的底层推理结构。

motivation.summary: 人类智能的基础是推理日常视觉输入的能力。虽然一些研究认为需要构建推理组件（如组合性或关系计算），但一个由通用组件构成的模型如果能学会视觉推理，将具有更广泛的适用性。

core_idea.summary: 引入一种通用的神经网络条件化方法FiLM（Feature-wise Linear Modulation）。FiLM层通过基于条件信息的简单、逐特征仿射变换来影响神经网络的计算，从而实现语言（问题）对视觉（图像）处理的自适应和根本性调制。

method.summary: 模型由FiLM生成器（语言管线）和FiLM化网络（视觉管线）组成。FiLM生成器（GRU）处理问题，为FiLM化网络（CNN）的每个残差块生成调制参数(γ, β)。FiLM层对CNN的中间特征图进行逐特征仿射变换：FiLM(F_{i,c} | γ_{i,c}, β_{i,c}) = γ_{i,c} * F_{i,c} + β_{i,c}。

experiments.summary: 在CLEVR基准上进行实验，包括主实验、消融研究、鲁棒性测试、泛化测试（CLEVR-Humans, CLEVR-CoGenT）和零样本泛化。

claims.claim: FiLM层在视觉推理任务上能将最先进误差减半。
FiLM以连贯的方式调制特征，学习复杂的底层结构。
FiLM对消融和架构修改具有鲁棒性。
FiLM模型能从少量数据中学习，并泛化到更复杂或不同的数据，甚至实现零样本泛化。
FiLM的成功与归一化没有紧密联系。

limitations.limitation: 论文未明确讨论局限性。潜在局限可能包括：在CLEVR等合成数据集上的成功不一定能直接迁移到更复杂的真实世界视觉推理任务；模型性能可能依赖于特定的架构选择（如残差块数量）；零样本泛化方法需要自动生成问题组合的解析器。

nodes.title: FiLM生成器
nodes.label: 语言处理模块
nodes.summary: 处理输入问题，生成用于调制视觉网络的FiLM参数(γ, β)。
nodes.description: FiLM生成器是一个GRU网络，具有4096个隐藏单元，接收200维的词嵌入。其最终隐藏状态作为问题嵌入，通过仿射投影为FiLM化网络的每个残差块预测(γ, β)参数。

nodes.title: FiLM化网络
nodes.label: 视觉处理模块
nodes.summary: 处理输入图像，并根据FiLM生成器提供的参数进行特征调制。
nodes.description: 视觉管线从调整大小的224x224图像中提取128个14x14的特征图，使用从头训练的CNN或固定的预训练特征提取器。网络包含多个FiLM化的残差块（ResBlock），每个块由1x1卷积和3x3卷积组成，并在卷积后应用FiLM层。网络末端使用全局最大池化和两层MLP（1024个隐藏单元）进行答案分类。

nodes.title: FiLM层
nodes.label: 核心调制操作
nodes.summary: 执行逐特征仿射变换，根据条件信息调制特征图。
nodes.description: FiLM层对目标网络的中间特征F_{i,c}应用变换：FiLM(F_{i,c} | γ_{i,c}, β_{i,c}) = γ_{i,c} * F_{i,c} + β_{i,c}。其中γ和β由FiLM生成器生成。该操作允许对特征图进行缩放、取反、关闭等操作。

nodes.title: 残差块（ResBlock）
nodes.label: FiLM化网络的基本单元
nodes.summary: 包含卷积层和FiLM层的残差学习块。
nodes.description: 每个FiLM化的残差块以1x1卷积开始，然后是一个3x3卷积，其后紧跟FiLM层。FiLM层位于卷积之后。模型使用坐标特征图（指示相对x和y空间位置）来辅助空间推理。

nodes.title: 分类器
nodes.label: 答案预测模块
nodes.summary: 基于调制后的视觉特征预测最终答案。
nodes.description: 由全局最大池化和两层MLP（1024个隐藏单元）组成，输出28个可能答案上的softmax分布。

edges.label: 生成调制参数
edges.summary: FiLM生成器为FiLM层提供γ和β参数。

edges.label: 提供待调制特征
edges.summary: FiLM化网络的中间特征图被传递给FiLM层进行调制。

edges.label: 调制残差块特征
edges.summary: FiLM层对残差块中的特征图进行调制。

edges.label: 传递调制后特征
edges.summary: 经过多个残差块处理后的特征被送入分类器。

deltas.before: 标准CNN/LSTM模型难以学习结构化、多步推理，倾向于利用数据偏差。
deltas.after: FiLM层通过语言条件化，自适应地、根本性地改变CNN的特征表示，使其能够执行多样化的多步推理任务。
deltas.why_it_matters: 使通用架构能够实现强大的视觉推理，无需显式建模推理过程，提高了模型的通用性和适用性。

deltas.before: 显式推理模型（如神经模块网络）需要强先验（如程序监督）和特定模块设计。
deltas.after: FiLM仅使用图像-问题-答案三元组进行端到端训练，无需额外监督或数据增强，通过简单的仿射变换实现灵活的特征调制。
deltas.why_it_matters: 简化了模型设计，减少了对领域特定知识和额外标注的依赖，同时保持了强大的性能。

deltas.before: 条件归一化方法（如条件批归一化）通常假设归一化与仿射变换紧密相关。
deltas.after: FiLM的消融研究表明，FiLM的成功与归一化没有紧密联系，可以独立于归一化层工作。
deltas.why_it_matters: 放宽了该方法的应用条件，使其更通用。

variables.name: \gamma_{i,c}
variables.description: 第i个输入的第c个特征图的缩放参数

variables.name: \beta_{i,c}
variables.description: 第i个输入的第c个特征图的偏移参数

variables.name: f_c, h_c
variables.description: 学习到的函数（例如神经网络），用于从输入x_i生成γ和β

formulas.intuition: FiLM生成器根据输入（如问题）为每个特征图独立地计算一对调制参数（缩放和偏移）。

variables.name: F_{i,c}
variables.description: 目标神经网络中第i个输入的第c个特征图的激活值

variables.name: \gamma_{i,c}, \beta_{i,c}
variables.description: 由FiLM生成器生成的调制参数

formulas.intuition: FiLM层的核心操作：对特征图的每个通道进行独立的仿射变换。通过调整γ和β，可以缩放、取反、关闭或选择性地阈值化特征图，从而根据条件信息（如问题）动态地改变网络的行为。

variables.name: \Delta\gamma_{i,c}
variables.description: γ的增量，用于避免初始时γ为零导致梯度消失

formulas.intuition: 实现细节：在实际实现中，输出的是Δγ而非直接输出γ，以确保初始时γ≈1，避免零中心化的γ在训练初期将特征图激活值置零，从而阻碍梯度流动。论文指出此修改对性能无显著影响。

main_result.description: 在CLEVR基准测试上，FiLM模型达到了97.7%的准确率，超越了人类水平和所有先前方法，包括使用额外监督或数据增强的方法。对于不使用额外监督的方法，FiLM将最先进误差从4.5%减半至2.3%。

ablation.description: 进行了广泛的消融研究，包括：1) 测试时消融（替换β为均值导致准确率下降1.0%，替换γ为均值导致下降65.4%，表明γ比β更重要）；2) 架构消融（如限制γ的范围、改变FiLM层位置）；3) 模型深度消融（不同数量的残差块）。大多数消融模型仍优于先前最先进方法。

robustness.description: FiLM对多种架构修改和测试时扰动具有鲁棒性。例如，即使限制γ的范围或改变FiLM层的位置，性能下降也相对较小。模型在不同深度（1-6个残差块）下表现稳定，尽管1个残差块时性能下降较大。

scaling.description: 研究了模型深度（残差块数量）对性能的影响。结果表明FiLM对深度变化鲁棒，但1个残差块时性能下降，支持了FiLM化网络在其整个管线中进行推理的观点。

case_study.description: 通过可视化分析（如特征图激活、FiLM参数分布、t-SNE图）展示了FiLM如何连贯地调制特征。例如，FiLM参数在不同层中按低级和高级推理功能聚类；模型能正确地定位问题相关的对象。

human_eval.description: 在CLEVR-Humans数据集上评估了模型的泛化能力。该数据集包含人类提出的更复杂、自由形式的问题。FiLM模型在微调后达到了75.9%的准确率，比先前最先进方法（PG+EE）高出9.3%，显示出更强的数据高效适应能力。

benchmark.description: 主要基准是CLEVR。此外，还在CLEVR-Humans和CLEVR-CoGenT上进行了评估。

efficiency.description: 论文提到FiLM是计算高效的条件化方法，因为每个调制的特征图只需要两个参数，其计算成本不随图像分辨率缩放。但未提供具体的训练/推理时间或FLOPs比较。

glossary.FiLM: Feature-wise Linear Modulation，一种通用的神经网络条件化方法，通过基于条件信息的逐特征仿射变换来调制网络的中间特征。
glossary.FiLM层: 执行FiLM操作的网络层，公式为 FiLM(F_{i,c} | γ_{i,c}, β_{i,c}) = γ_{i,c} * F_{i,c} + β_{i,c}。
glossary.FiLM生成器: 生成FiLM调制参数(γ, β)的网络部分，在本文中是一个处理问题的GRU网络。
glossary.FiLM化网络: 被FiLM层调制的目标网络部分，在本文中是处理图像的CNN。
glossary.CLEVR: 一个用于评估视觉推理能力的合成数据集，包含3D渲染的物体图像和多步、组合性的问题。
glossary.残差块（ResBlock）: FiLM化网络中的基本构建块，包含卷积层和FiLM层，并具有残差连接。
glossary.条件归一化: 一类方法，其仿射变换（如批归一化中的缩放和偏移）是基于条件信息生成的。FiLM是一种更通用的条件化形式。
glossary.零样本泛化: 模型处理在训练期间未见过的概念组合的能力。本文通过在FiLM参数空间中进行线性组合来实现。

required_models: CNN（从头训练或预训练特征提取器）
reproduction.compute: 论文提到在CLEVR上训练80个epoch，但未提供具体的GPU类型、数量或训练时间。需要中等规模的计算资源。
reproduction.code_available: 是，代码在 https://github.com/ethanjperez/film 提供。

steps.description: 1. 准备数据集：下载并预处理CLEVR、CLEVR-Humans、CLEVR-CoGenT数据集。
2. 实现FiLM生成器：构建GRU网络，接收词嵌入，输出(γ, β)参数。
3. 实现FiLM化网络：构建包含多个残差块的CNN，每个残差块后接FiLM层。添加坐标特征图。
4. 实现分类器：全局最大池化后接两层MLP。
5. 端到端训练：使用Adam优化器（学习率3e-4），权重衰减1e-5，批大小64，早停法（基于验证准确率），最多80个epoch。
6. 进行消融和泛化实验：按照论文描述进行各种消融研究和在CLEVR-Humans、CLEVR-CoGenT上的评估。

metadata.title: FiLM: Visual Reasoning with a General Conditioning Layer
metadata.paper_type: Computer Vision / Pose Estimation / Computer Vision / Top-cited Computer Vision paper
metadata.abstract: We introduce a general-purpose conditioning method for neural networks called FiLM: Feature-wise Linear Modulation. FiLM layers influence neural network computation via a simple, feature-wise affine transformation based on conditioning information. We show that FiLM layers are highly effective for visual reasoning - answering image-related questions which require a multi-step, high-level process - a task which has proven difficult for standard deep learning methods that do not explicitly model reasoning. Specifically, we show on visual reasoning tasks that FiLM layers 1) halve state-of-the-art error for the CLEVR benchmark, 2) modulate features in a coherent manner, 3) are robust to ablations and architectural modifications, and 4) generalize well to challenging, new data from few examples or even zero-shot.

anchors.text_span: FiLM: Visual Reasoning with a General Conditioning Layer Ethan Perez1,2, Florian Strub4, Harm de Vries1, Vincent Dumoulin1, Aaron Courville1,3 1MILA, Universit´e de Montr´eal, 2Rice University, 3CIFAR Fellow, 4Univ. Lille, CNRS, Centrale Lille, Inria, UMR 9189 CRIStAL France ethanperez@rice.edu, ﬂorian.strub@inria.fr, mail@harmdevries.com,{dumouliv,courvila}@iro.umontreal.ca
Abstract

We introduce a general-purpose conditioning method for neu- ral networks called FiLM: Feature-wise Linear Modulation. FiLM layers inﬂuence neural network computation via a sim- ple, feature-wise afﬁne transformation based on conditioning information. We show that FiLM layers are highly effective for visual reasoning — answering image-related questions which require a multi-step, high-level process — a task which has proven difﬁcult for standard deep learning methods that do not explicitly model reasoning. Speciﬁcally, we show on visual reasoning tasks that FiLM layers 1) halve state-of-the- art error for the CLEVR benchmark, 2) modulate features in a coherent manner, 3) are robust to ablations and architectural modiﬁcations, and 4) generalize well to challenging, new data from few examples or even zero-shot.
1 Introduction
The ability to reason about everyday visual input is a fun- damental building block of human intelligence. Some have
argued that for artiﬁcial agents to learn this complex, struc-

tured process, it is necessary to build in aspects of reason- ing, such as compositionality (Hu et al. 2017; Johnson et al. 2017b) or relational computation (Santoro et al. 2017). However, if a model made from general-purpose compo- nents could learn to visually reason, such an architecture would likely be more widely applicable across domains. To understand if such a general-purpose architecture ex- ists, we take advantage of the recently proposed CLEVR dataset (Johnson et al. 2017a) that tests visual reasoning via question answering. Examples from CLEVR are shown in
Figure 1. Visual question answering, the general task of ask-

ing questions about images, has its own line of datasets (Ma- linowski and Fritz 2014; Geman et al. 2015; Antol et al. 2015) which generally focus on asking a diverse set of simpler questions on images, often answerable in a single glance. From these datasets, a number of effective, general- purpose deep learning models have emerged for visual ques- tion answering (Malinowski, Rohrbach, and Fritz 2015; Yang et al. 2016; Lu et al. 2016; Anderson et al. 2017). How- ever, tests on CLEVR show that these general deep learning approaches struggle to learn structured, multi-step reason- ing (Johnson et al. 2017a). In this work, we show that a general model architecture can achieve strong visual reasoning with a method we intro- duce as FiLM: Feature-wise Linear Modulation. A FiLM layer carries out a simple, feature-wise afﬁne transformation on a neural network’s intermediate features, conditioned on an arbitrary input. In the case of visual reasoning, FiLM lay- ers enable a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) over an input question to inﬂuence Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) computation over an image. This process adaptively and rad- ically alters the CNN’s behavior as a function of the input question, allowing the overall model to carry out a variety of reasoning tasks, ranging from counting to comparing, for example. 2 Method
Our model processes the question-image input using FiLM, illustrated in Figure 2. We start by explaining FiLM and then describe our particular model for visual reasoning.
2.1 Feature-wise Linear Modulation

FiLM learns to adaptively inﬂuence the output of a neural network by applying an afﬁne transformation, or FiLM, to the network’s intermediate features, based on some input. More formally, FiLM learns functionsf andh which output γi,c andβi,c as a function of inputxi:
γi,c =fc(xi) βi,c =hc(xi), (1)
whereγi,c andβi,c modulate a neural network’s activations Fi,c, whose subscripts refer to the ith input’scth feature or feature map, via a feature-wise afﬁne transformation:
FiLM (Fi,c|γi,c,β i,c) = γi,cFi,c +βi,c. (2)
f andh can be arbitrary functions such as neural networks.
Modulation of a target neural network’s processing can be

based on the same input to that neural network or some other input, as in the case of multi-modal or conditional tasks. For CNNs,f andh thus modulate the per-feature-map distribu- tion of activations based onxi, agnostic to spatial location. In practice, it is easier to refer tof andh as a single func- tion that outputs one (γ,β) vector, since, for example, it is often beneﬁcial to share parameters across f and h for more efﬁcient learning. We refer to this single function as the FiLM generator. We also refer to the network to which FiLM layers are applied as the Feature-wise Linearly Mod- ulated network, the FiLM-ed network. FiLM layers empower the FiLM generator to manipulate
feature maps of a target, FiLM-ed network by scaling them

up or down, negating them, shutting them off, selectively thresholding them (when followed by a ReLU), and more. Each feature map is conditioned independently, giving the FiLM generator moderately ﬁne-grained control over acti- vations at each FiLM layer. As FiLM only requires two parameters per modulated fea- ture map, it is a scalable and computationally efﬁcient con- ditioning method. In particular, FiLM has a computational cost that does not scale with the image resolution.

2.2 Model
Our FiLM model consists of a FiLM-generating linguis- tic pipeline and a FiLM-ed visual pipeline as depicted in
Figure 3. The FiLM generator processes a question xi us-

ing a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network (Chung et al. 2014) with 4096 hidden units that takes in learned, 200- dimensional word embeddings. The ﬁnal GRU hidden state is a question embedding, from which the model predicts (γn i,·,βn i,·) for eachnth residual block via afﬁne projection. The visual pipeline extracts 128 14× 14 image feature maps from a resized, 224× 224 image input using either a CNN trained from scratch or a ﬁxed, pre-trained feature extractor with a learned layer of 3× 3 convolutions. The CNN trained from scratch consists of 4 layers with 128 4× 4 kernels each, ReLU activations, and batch normalization, similar to prior work on CLEVR (Santoro et al. 2017). The ﬁxed feature extractor outputs the conv4 layer of a ResNet- 101 (He et al. 2016) pre-trained on ImageNet (Russakovsky et al. 2015) to match prior work on CLEVR (Johnson et al. 2017a; 2017b). 3 Related Work

FiLM can be viewed as a generalization of Conditional Nor- malization (CN) methods. CN replaces the parameters of the feature-wise afﬁne transformation typical in normalization layers, as introduced originally (Ioffe and Szegedy 2015), with a learned function of some conditioning information. Various forms of CN have proven highly effective across a number of domains: Conditional Instance Norm (Dumoulin, Shlens, and Kudlur 2017; Ghiasi et al. 2017) and Adaptive Instance Norm (Huang and Belongie 2017) for image styl- ization, Dynamic Layer Norm for speech recognition (Kim, Song, and Bengio 2017), and Conditional Batch Norm for general visual question answering on complex scenes such as VQA and GuessWhat?! (de Vries et al. 2017). This work complements our own, as we seek to show that feature-wise afﬁne conditioning is effective for multi-step reasoning and understand the underlying mechanism behind its success.
Notably, prior work in CN has not examined whether

the afﬁne transformation must be placed directly after nor- malization. Rather, prior work includes normalization in the method name for instructive purposes or due to implemen- tation details. We investigate the connection between FiLM and normalization, ﬁnding it not strictly necessary for the afﬁne transformation to occur directly after normalization. Thus, we provide a uniﬁed framework for all of these meth- ods through FiLM, as well as a normalization-free relaxation of this approach which can be more broadly applied. Beyond CN, there are many connections between FiLM and other conditioning methods. A common approach, used for example in Conditional DCGANs (Radford, Metz, and Chintala 2016), is to concatenate constant feature maps of conditioning information with convolutional layer input. Though not as parameter efﬁcient, this method simply re- sults in a feature-wise conditional bias. Likewise, concate- nating conditioning information with fully-connected layer input amounts to...
equivalent to FiLM with γ = 1, which we compare FiLM

to in the Experiments section. In reinforcement learning, an alternate formulation of FiLM has been used to train one game-conditioned deep Q-network to play ten Atari games (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017), though FiLM was neither the focus of this work nor analyzed as a major component. Other methods gate an input’s features as a function of that same input, rather than a separate conditioning in- put. These methods include LSTMs for sequence model- ing (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997), Convolutional Se- quence to Sequence for machine translation (Gehring et al. 2017), and even the ImageNet 2017 winning model, Squeeze and Excitation Networks (Hu, Shen, and Sun 2017). This approach amounts to a feature-wise, conditional scaling, re- stricted to between 0 and 1, while FiLM consists of both scaling and shifting, each unrestricted. 4 Experiments

First, we test our model on visual reasoning with the CLEVR task and use trained FiLM models to analyze what FiLM learns. Second, we explore how well our model generalizes to more challenging questions with the CLEVR-Humans
task. Finally, we examine how FiLM performs in few-

shot and zero-shot generalization settings using the CLEVR Compositional Generalization Test. In the appendix, we pro- vide an error analysis of our model. Our code is available at https://github.com/ethanjperez/film.
4.1 CLEVR Task

CLEVR is a synthetic dataset of 700K (image, question, an- swer, program) tuples (Johnson et al. 2017a). Images con- tain 3D-rendered objects of various shapes, materials, col- ors, and sizes. Questions are multi-step and compositional in nature, as shown in Figure 1. They range from counting questions (“How many green objects have the same size as the green metallic block?” ) to comparison questions ( “Are there fewer tiny yellow cylinders than yellow metal cubes?”) and can be 40+ words long. Answers are each one word from a set of 28 possible answers. Programs are an additional supervisory signal consisting of step-by-step instructions, such as filter shape[cube], relate[right], and count, on how to answer the question. Repetitive Conditioning To understand the contribution of repetitive conditioning towards FiLM model success, we train FiLM models with successively fewer FiLM layers. Models with fewer FiLM layers, even a single FiLM layer, do not deviate far from the best model’s performance, reveal- ing that the model can reason and answer diverse questions successfully by modulating features even just once. 5 Conclusion

We show that a model can achieve strong visual reasoning using general-purpose Feature-wise Linear Modulation lay- ers. By efﬁciently manipulating a neural network’s interme- diate features in a selective and meaningful manner using FiLM layers, a RNN can effectively use language to mod- ulate a CNN to carry out diverse and multi-step reasoning tasks over an image. Our ablation study suggests that FiLM is resilient to architectural modiﬁcations, test time ablations, and even restrictions on FiLM layers themselves. Notably, we provide evidence that FiLM’s success is not closely con- nected with normalization as previously assumed. Thus, we open the door for applications of this approach to settings where normalization is less common, such as RNNs and re- inforcement learning. Our ﬁndings also suggest that FiLM models can generalize better, more sample efﬁciently, and even zero-shot to foreign or more challenging data. 7 Appendix
7.1 Error Analysis
We examine the errors our model makes to understand where our

model fails and how it acts when it does. Examples of these errors are shown in Figures 12 and 13. Occlusion Many model errors are due to partial occlusion. These errors may likely be ﬁxed using a CNN that operates at a higher resolution, which is feasible since FiLM has a computa- tional cost that is independent of resolution. Counting 96.1% of counting mistakes are off-by-one errors, showing FiLM has learned underlying concepts behind counting such as close relationships between close numbers. Logical Consistency The model sometimes makes curious reasoning mistakes a human would not. For example, we ﬁnd a case where our model correctly counts one gray object and two cyan objects but simultaneously answers that there are the same number of gray and cyan objects. In fact, it answers that the num- ber of gray objects is both less than and equal to the number of
yellow blocks. These errors could be prevented by directly mini-
mizing logical inconsistency, an interesting avenue for future work
orthogonal to FiLM.
7.2 Model Details
Rather than outputγi,c directly, we output ∆γi,c, where:

since initially zero-centered γi,c can zero out CNN feature map activations and thus gradients. In our implementation, we opt to output ∆γi,c rather thanγi,c, but for simplicity, throughout our pa- per, we explain FiLM using γi,c. However, this modiﬁcation does not seem to affect our model’s performance on CLEVR statistically signiﬁcantly. We present training and validation curves for best model trained from image features in Figure 11. We observe fast accuracy gains initially, followed by slow, steady increases to a best validation ac- curacy of 97.84%, at which point training accuracy is 99.53%. We train on CLEVR for 80 epochs, which takes 4 days using 1 NVIDIA TITAN Xp GPU when learning from image features. For practical reasons, we stop training on CLEVR after 80 epochs, but we observe that accuracy continues to increase slowly even after- wards.
